cover.headline: Refrigerants are carrying SRF while specialty chemicals stall: fairly priced, not a bargain
cover.lead: SRF makes refrigerant gases, chemical building blocks for global agrochemical and pharma companies, packaging films and tyre cord. Chemicals are half of revenue and three-quarters of profit. The record FY26 and first half of FY27 came from two things: refrigerant prices at a decade high as quotas tighten supply worldwide, and a one-off windfall in films during the Middle East war. Specialty chemicals, the growth engine of FY19-23, has shrunk for two years under Chinese overcapacity. We value SRF the way the street does, on the **sum of its parts: Sep-28E EV/EBITDA, with chemicals at 20x**. That gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** A P/E cross-check (28x Sep-28E EPS of ₹92.5) lands in the same place; the DCF (₹1,548) warns that cash flows alone support much less while capex runs at ₹2,500 cr a year. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Refrigerants: a quota-protected boom, close to its peak?
arguments.p: Fluorochemical revenue rose 60% in FY26 to ₹3,598 cr. China caps HFC production and its R32 price hit a decade high in 2026. India's own HFC quotas, from 2028, will be based on 2024-26 output, so SRF has run its plants flat out. But calendar 2027 is a "free year" in which new Indian capacity can sell, and UBS argues prices are near the peak.

arguments.h: Specialty chemicals, the long-term story, is stuck
arguments.p: Specialty revenue fell from ₹4,165 cr in FY23 to ₹3,537 cr in FY26 as Chinese overcapacity cut prices and agrochemical customers ran down stock. In Q2FY27 the chemicals EBIT margin fell to 25.4% from 28.9%, all of it from specialty (Kotak). 7-8 new agro molecules are "in an advanced state", but their timing depends on customers' registrations, and they have been "close" for three years.

arguments.h: Capex: chemicals has earned its money; films has not
arguments.p: Since FY21 chemicals capital rose ₹5,537 cr and earned a 28% pre-tax return on it. Films capital nearly doubled while its profit fell. The next ₹2,500 cr a year goes mainly into HFOs, fluoropolymers and battery foil, with the pay-off in FY28-29.

arguments.h: Valuation: the market already pays ~18x for chemicals
arguments.p: Brokers value chemicals at 15-23x EV/EBITDA. After valuing the other businesses at our multiples, today's price implies ~18.0x Sep-28E for chemicals; our 20x leaves only modest upside. The stock has de-rated from 48x forward earnings (2021-25 median) to ~28.8x FY27E, which is why it is not expensive either.

catalysts: Q3FY27 results (Jan-2027): evidence of the promised H2 specialty recovery.
India's HFC quota rules (final view expected early 2027) and refrigerant prices in the 2027 "free year".
Commissioning: PVDF (Q3FY27), Chemours fluoropolymer plants (Q4FY27, Q1FY28), Odisha HFO plant (Q4FY28).
Promoter KAMA Holdings has approval to sell up to 3% by Mar-2027 (so far only an internal transfer).
Sunset review of the anti-dumping duty on Chinese R32 (Dec-2026).

sections.title: Four businesses: one chemicals franchise and three industrial ones

blocks.p: SRF started in 1973 making nylon tyre cord, added refrigerant gases in 1989 and packaging films in 1995, and moved into complex chemicals for global agrochemical and pharma companies from 2004. Today it runs 16 plants in India, Thailand, South Africa and Hungary. Half its revenue is exported. The four businesses look very different on growth, margins and returns, which is why the market values each one separately.

blocks.h: Inside chemicals: two very different businesses

blocks.p: **Fluorochemicals** (₹3,598 cr of FY26 product revenue) are refrigerant gases for air-conditioners, fridges and car ACs, plus industrial chemicals and fluoropolymers. Prices follow a global commodity cycle shaped by regulation: as countries phase down climate-warming HFC gases, supply is rationed by quota, which lifts prices for those who hold quota. **Specialty chemicals** (₹3,537 cr) are custom-made intermediates and active ingredients for global agrochemical (and, increasingly, pharma) innovators. This is a contract business: SRF develops a process for a customer's molecule and supplies it for years. It earns better margins in good times, but it has lost pricing to Chinese makers since FY24 and depends on customers' launch timetables.

sections.title: Refrigerants are rationed by regulation; specialty and films are not

blocks.p: HFC refrigerants are powerful greenhouse gases, so the 2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol makes every country phase them down. That turns a commodity into a quota business: once production is capped, holders of quota earn more. **China**, the largest producer, has capped HFC output since 2024 (797,800 tonnes in 2026, with the top six firms holding ~90%), and its R32 price reached a decade high of ~CNY 63,000 a tonne in 2026. **India** freezes HFC production from 1 January 2028 at a baseline set by 2024-26 output, which is why SRF has run its plants flat out and is debottlenecking to over 65,000 tonnes a year. The catch is **calendar 2027**: a "free year" in which anyone with capacity may sell before the quotas start.

bullets: **Refrigerants.** Q1FY27 was helped by a harsh global summer and full plants; Q2FY27 chemicals revenue was still +25% on higher HFC volumes and prices, with Middle East sales replacing a softer US (where R32 now faces tariffs). Management expects refrigerant demand and prices to stay "broadly stable". SRF will not disclose capacity; analysts estimate ~27-28k tonnes of R32 against Indian demand of 17-18k tonnes, so a large share is exported.

**Specialty.** "Linear, slow recovery", says management: H2FY27 should be stronger than H1 on volumes, and "the worst of price destruction is behind". Pharma is ~10% of specialty today; the target is 20-30% by 2030, with two Western innovators (one oncology molecule) about to contribute. 7-8 agro products are "in a very advanced state" with customers; registrations for two are progressing in Brazil.

**Fluoropolymers.** PTFE is shifting to value-added grades; PVDF (batteries, coatings) is being capitalised in Q3FY27; two plants built for Chemours (FEP/FKM) start in Q4FY27 and Q1FY28 on a return-on-investment contract, reaching full run-rate in FY29.

**HFOs.** The ₹2,300 cr Odisha project (20,000 tonnes of HFOs plus hydrofluoric acid) uses SRF's own non-infringing process and is due in Q4FY28. HFOs sell at "significantly" higher prices than HFCs. Meaningful volumes come 8-12 months after start-up, i.e. in FY29.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** chemicals is a good business. Its pre-tax ROCE has been 17-28% since FY22, and new capital since FY21 has earned 28%. But FY26-27 profits sit at the top of the refrigerant cycle, while the specialty recovery keeps being pushed out. We model chemicals growth of 19% / 12% / 16% (FY27-29E) and an EBITDA margin of ~32-33%, below FY26's 35.7%.

bullets: **Films & foil** (37% of FY26 revenue, 17% of segment EBIT). Commodity BOPET/BOPP films made in India, Thailand, South Africa, Hungary and Indonesia. Margins collapsed from 27% EBIT in FY21 to 4.6% in FY24 when the industry added far more capacity than demand. In Q1FY27 the Middle East war shut rival plants, customers panic-bought and SRF earned 17.3%; Q2 fell back to 9.7%. Management says the "baseline" should settle higher as it moves to value-added products: capacitor films, BOPA, thick BOPET and aluminium foil (₹568 cr revenue in FY26, to turn profitable by the end of FY27; a ₹600 cr battery-foil plant from 2028).

**Technical textiles** (12% of revenue). India's #1 tyre-cord maker (60,000 tonnes) and a large belting-fabric exporter. EBIT margin fell from 22.6% in FY22 to 10.1% in FY26 on cheap imports and US tariffs; H1FY27 recovered to 15% as US tariffs were cut and a quality-control order protected industrial yarn.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** SRF's moat is **fluorine chemistry plus regulation**: it can run hazardous fluorination at scale, it owns processes (including a non-infringing HFO route), Chemours chose it as a partner, and India's quota system will lock in existing producers from 2028. That is a genuine, durable advantage. But in **specialty chemicals** China is cheaper and customers choose who makes their molecules; and **films** are a commodity. Two-thirds of the business is therefore cyclical, which is why SRF's ROE swings with the cycle (25% in FY22, 10% in FY25, 14% in FY26) instead of compounding steadily like the best Indian chemical franchises.

sections.title: Six years of growth, two lost years, and now a record half

blocks.p: SRF's revenue rose from ₹4,822 cr in FY17 to ₹14,870 cr in FY23, about 21% a year, as the chemicals business grew from a refrigerant maker into a supplier of complex molecules to global agrochemical and pharma companies. Then the cycle turned. In FY24 revenue fell 12% and net profit fell 38%, and FY25 was weaker still (₹1,251 cr). FY26 was a partial recovery (₹1,835 cr). The first half of FY27 is the best in SRF's history: revenue up 33% and net profit ₹1,268 cr, already 69% of all of FY26.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** SRF is a capital-heavy compounder. Gross block went from ₹4,963 cr in FY17 to ₹19,229 cr in FY26, and depreciation from ₹283 cr to ₹852 cr. Each new plant adds fixed cost before it adds profit, so earnings jump when plants fill up and prices are firm (FY21-23, H1FY27), and fall hard when either slips (FY24-25).

sections.title: ₹15,600 cr of capex in ten years: returns have not kept up

blocks.p: Over FY17-26 SRF generated ₹17,438 cr of operating cash and spent ₹15,594 cr on new plants: 89 paise of every rupee. After ₹1,546 cr of dividends there was almost nothing left, so borrowings doubled from ₹2,396 cr to ₹5,083 cr. That is fine if the new capacity earns well. The test is return on capital employed (ROCE): it peaked at 24% in FY22, fell to 12% in FY25 and was 15% in FY26, about SRF's cost of capital.

pair.title: ROCE: back to 15%, below the FY22 peak
pair.source: Screener.in

blocks.callout: **Where it went right and wrong:** split by business, the picture is sharper. Since FY21, capital employed in **chemicals** rose by ₹5,537 cr and its EBIT by ₹1,535 cr: a 28% pre-tax return on the new money. In **films**, capital employed nearly doubled (₹3,425 cr to ₹6,310 cr) while EBIT fell from ₹898 cr to ₹508 cr. Group ROCE fell because of films, not chemicals. CWIP (plants being built) jumped to ₹2,122 cr by Sep-2026, and this round of spending is mostly in chemicals (HFOs, fluoropolymers).

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books, but hedging losses and one-offs to strip out

bullets: **Forex hedge losses.** SRF sells forward its export dollars for long periods. As the rupee weakened, these hedges lost ₹119 cr in FY25, ₹188 cr in FY26 and ₹165 cr in H1FY27. The company reports them below its own EBITDA; Screener (and this report) treats them as an operating cost. That is why Q2FY27 EBITDA is ₹946 cr here and ~₹1,010 cr in some broker notes.

**One-offs.** FY26 included an ₹85 cr exceptional charge for the new Labour Codes and a ₹99 cr tax credit from a favourable tribunal order (Q3FY26). Q1FY27 films and textiles margins included low-cost inventory gains that reversed in Q2.
**Corporate costs.** Segment EBIT (₹3,008 cr in FY26) is before ₹343 cr of unallocated costs (net of other income). Sum-of-the-parts valuations that ignore this flatter the result; ours deducts it.
**Depreciation before revenue.** New plants are capitalised and depreciated a couple of quarters before they earn. With ₹2,122 cr in CWIP, depreciation will keep rising ahead of profits.

**Audit.** B S R & Co. (KPMG network) gives a clean opinion; its key audit matter is hedge accounting. It notes that edit logs were not enabled on some accounting master tables during FY26 (a common IT-controls remark).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Segment disclosure is detailed and reconciles to reported profit; the auditor is a Big-4 firm with no qualification. Hedge losses and one-offs are disclosed clearly; investors simply need to strip them out.

sections.title: Moderate debt, working capital rising with sales

blocks.p: Net debt (borrowings less cash and investments) was ₹3,785 cr at March 2026, about 1.1x EBITDA: comfortable for a company of this size. Working capital is the other use of cash. Inventory days (131) and receivable days (59) are high because SRF holds raw materials, refrigerant stock for the cooling season and finished intermediates for global customers. In the six months to Sep-2026 inventory rose ₹590 cr and receivables ₹599 cr as sales jumped, and borrowings rose to ₹5,375 cr.

sections.title: Ownership: domestic funds are replacing foreign investors

blocks.p: The Bharat Ram family controls SRF through KAMA Holdings (listed), which with a group company owns 50.26%, with no shares pledged. sections.title: Our forecasts: in line for FY27, below the street for FY28

blocks.p: We forecast each segment's revenue and EBITDA margin (segment EBIT plus its depreciation). Group EBITDA is the sum less corporate costs and hedge losses. Capex follows guidance (₹2,500 cr in FY27, more in FY28 for the HFO plant), so depreciation and interest rise ahead of the new plants' profits. Every assumption, with our reasoning, is in the Excel model's Assumptions sheet, which recalculates this report's target price.

exhibit.title: Group P&L and cash flow summary (₹ crore)

blocks.callout: For FY27 we are in line with consensus: H1 already delivered ₹1,268 cr of profit. For FY28 our EPS is ~5% below the street because we assume (1) refrigerant prices soften in the 2027 "free year", and (2) films margins fall back as war-time prices fade. FY29 recovers on HFOs and fluoropolymers if they start on time; that is the swing factor.

sections.title: The street: split after the Q2 miss

blocks.p: After the Q2FY27 results (22-Oct-2026) the street is split: 2 Buys (Motilal Oswal, ICICI Direct), 2 Holds (Prabhudas Lilladher, Jefferies) and 3 Sells (Kotak, UBS, Morgan Stanley). Targets range from ₹2,210 to ₹3,000. The broader consensus (29 analysts, MarketScreener) still averages ₹2,788, but much of it predates the miss. Bulls point to refrigerants, fluoropolymers and HFOs; bears to Chinese specialty pricing, peak refrigerant prices and a long wait for capex to pay off.

exhibit.title: Critiques we take seriously
head: Argument
Who
rows: Refrigerant prices are near a cyclical peak; the HFC-to-HFO and supply-tightness tailwinds are already priced in - mean reversion risk.

Specialty chemicals (largest chemicals sub-business pre-FY26) faces structural Chinese overcapacity; the entire Q2FY27 chemicals margin decline came from specialty; earnings acceleration may wait till FY29 and valuations still look full.
Specialty challenges could persist longer than anticipated - chemicals multiple should be cut to 20x from 25x; the Street is not convinced of the promised H2 recovery.
Subdued agrochemical demand and persistent Chinese oversupply keep the stock a Hold even after the correction.
AI/new-molecule commercialisation keeps slipping (talked about for ~3 years); depends on innovators' registrations - timing uncertain "to say it mildly".
ICICI Securities analyst question; management answer (Jul-2026)
Valuation stretched historically (47x forward P/E, >2 SD above average in Feb-2025) with EPS estimates 16-17% below consensus.
Downside risk to consensus from Chinese pricing pressure and delays in key product commercialisation; margin sustainability doubtful.
Q1FY27 record was a one-off (war-driven film supply shortage, panic buying, inventory gains); Q2 films margin fell back to 9.7%.

sections.title: Valuation: sum of the parts gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}

blocks.p: Brokers value SRF as **four businesses on EV/EBITDA** (enterprise value to operating profit), because chemicals deserves a far higher multiple than films or tyre cord. Every broker whose method we could find, except Elara (DCF), uses this sum of the parts on FY28-29E EBITDA. They differ mainly on the chemicals multiple: from 15x (Kotak) to 23x (Motilal Oswal). We use the same method, so our target is comparable; the last column shows each broker's multiples applied to our own estimates.

The DCF is 40% lower: with ₹2,500 cr a year of capex, free cash flow is thin until FY29, and at a 12.5% cost of capital the cash flows alone do not support today's price. The market (and our target) is paying for HFOs and fluoropolymers to lift returns from FY29. If they slip, the multiple has room to fall.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good chemicals business at a fair price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's leading fluorochemicals maker, with a quota-protected refrigerant business, real process know-how and a pipeline of new products (HFOs, fluoropolymers, battery foil). Attached are three cyclical, low-return businesses (specialty chemicals today, films and tyre cord).

**What you are paying:** 27.8x FY28E earnings and ~18.0x Sep-28E EBITDA for chemicals, well below SRF's own history. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): short of our 15% BUY threshold. Profits today rest on refrigerant prices that may be at a peak; the next leg needs specialty to recover and HFOs to start on time.

**Biggest swing factor:** the refrigerant price. It made FY26 and could unmake FY28.

sections.title: Annotated financials
Glossary

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Hydrofluorocarbon: today's main refrigerant gases (e.g. R32 for home ACs, R134a for car ACs, R125 for blends). Powerful greenhouse gases, now being phased down.
Hydrofluoro-olefin: next-generation refrigerants with very low global-warming impact; replacing HFCs in cars and, gradually, ACs.
The 2016 global agreement to cut HFC production and use, country by country, through quotas.
The production level on which a country's quotas are based; for India the 2024-26 average, frozen from 2028.
SRF's term for calendar 2027: after the baseline period but before quotas apply, so any producer may sell.
(Anhydrous) hydrofluoric acid: the basic raw material for all fluorochemicals.
Fluoropolymers: plastics and rubbers made from fluorine chemistry, used in cables, batteries, semiconductors and seals.
Making a specific intermediate or active ingredient for one agrochemical or pharma innovator under a long-term contract.
A company that discovers and patents new molecules (e.g. a global agrochemical major) and outsources some manufacturing.
Types of plastic packaging film (polyester, polypropylene, nylon, cast polypropylene).
Nylon or polyester fabric that reinforces tyres.
Loss on forward contracts that lock in the rupee value of future export earnings, when the rupee weakens.
Valuing each business separately and adding them up, less net debt.
Enterprise value (market value plus net debt) divided by operating profit before depreciation.
Return on capital employed: operating profit (EBIT) as % of the capital tied up in the business.
Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash.
